Losing our first big customer was the best thing that ever happened to Ledgerline.

Let me explain.

5 months in, they walked away. It stung. A lot.

But failure isn't the opposite of success. It's part of it.

The reason they left: they had heavily customized their NetSuite instance, and we only supported standard fields. We weren't meeting them where they were.

So we did what good teams do. We listened, we learned, and we built. We spent 6 weeks adding support for custom fields. It was more than a feature; it changed how we think about our customers.

Today we serve 38 customers, and 11 of them rely on custom fields.

The lesson: your biggest setback can become your biggest breakthrough. Lean into the hard feedback. Your customers are telling you what to build — you just have to listen.

What loss shaped your company?

#Startups #SaaS #Leadership #CustomerSuccess #Growth

We built a beautiful app. Nobody used it.

When we launched Rotaship, we were proud of our sleek, modern mobile app. We assumed restaurant staff would love it.

Reality check: only 12% of staff even opened it in the first month.

That's when it hit us. We weren't solving the real problem. We were adding another one.

Restaurant teams don't want another app. They live on WhatsApp.

So in 2025, we made a tough call and moved everything into WhatsApp.

The results speak for themselves: 140 outlets, with a median reply time to shift messages under 20 minutes.

The lesson? Meet your users where they already are. Don't make them come to you.

Sometimes the best product decision is letting go of the thing you love.

1,200 repositories.

When we launched Patchwork CI, we made a promise: always free for open source. A lot of people told us we were crazy. "How will you make money?" they asked.

Today we're running on 1,200 repositories, and about 900 of them are open source.

Why we stopped billing by the hour and never looked back.

When we started Fernway Studio, we did what every agency does: we charged hourly.

The result? 4 of our first 6 projects went over budget.

Clients were frustrated. We were frustrated. Trust was eroding.

So in 2024, we made a bold decision. We switched to a fixed price: KES 450,000 per Shopify store. Period.

And it changed everything.

Clients know exactly what they're paying.
We're incentivized to work smarter, not longer.
Relationships are built on trust, not timesheets.

Since then, we've launched 31 stores. Only 2 went over our 6-week timeline.

Pricing isn't just a number. It's a promise.

Founders, how do you price your services? Let me know in the comments.
